speaker: Steven Strogatz
title: Steven Strogatz on the Humanity of Math | 3b1b Podcast
question: In pure mathematics, why do researchers care far more about certain famous unsolved conjectures than about other equally simple ones?
guest: There's power in the outside world, but there's also being generative in the inside world—generative of more ideas, math that keeps posing new questions. Take the quest to prove Fermat's Last Theorem. Pure mathematicians love that story because along the way to solving it, they invented ideals in algebra, discovered number fields without unique prime factorization, and built a whole glorious world around it that is arguably more important than Fermat's Last Theorem itself. That conjecture was a lighthouse: trying to solve it created ideas that took on a life of their own and led toward the Langlands program and modular forms. By contrast, Goldbach's conjecture—that every even number is the sum of two primes—seems in a way like a simpler question, yet very few mathematicians get excited about it because it hasn't been as generative. It's peripheral, not connecting to the great body of other math. As Gauss noted, it's easy to make up a question you can neither prove nor refute that isn't connected to anything else, and that's of little interest.

points.core: Mathematicians value a conjecture primarily for the new mathematical machinery it generates.
points.note: Accept: generativity, spawning new theories/tools/structures (such as ideals, number fields, or modular forms), or acting as a guiding lighthouse whose surrounding framework matters more than the binary proof. Do not credit: generic claims about fame, prize money, or historical prestige.

points.core: Deep conjectures connect productively to major central frameworks across broader mathematics.
points.note: Accept: bridging disparate subfields, linking to unifying programs like Langlands, or illuminating structural relationships across the mathematical landscape. Do not credit: saying a problem is simply 'harder' or 'more famous'.

points.core: Isolated puzzles disconnected from wider theory attract little interest despite simple statements.
points.note: Accept: peripheral conjectures (such as Goldbach's conjecture) that are easy to state yet fail to spawn rich surrounding superstructure or connect to core math. Do not credit: claiming simple problems are unpopular because they are too easy.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Mathematicians value a conjecture less for its statement than for what it connects to and what proving it would require. A problem becomes important when it sits at the centre of a web of other mathematics.

The Riemann Hypothesis matters because hundreds of theorems are proved conditionally on it, and it governs the distribution of primes. Fermat's Last Theorem, itself a fairly isolated statement, became central once it was tied to the modularity of elliptic curves, and its proof reshaped number theory. The Langlands conjectures matter because they unify whole fields.

By contrast, a simple-sounding problem like the Collatz conjecture, or whether odd perfect numbers exist, attracts less serious effort. Few consequences would follow from a solution, and no existing theory seems to get a grip on it, so work on it rarely produces useful partial results.

Researchers therefore favour problems that are consequential (many things follow), structural (they reveal why something is true, not just that it is), and tractable enough that failed attempts still generate new tools. History and prestige play a part too: famous names, prizes and long resistance amplify attention.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Mathematicians judge an unsolved conjecture not by the simplicity of its statement, but by its connectivity, consequences, and power to generate new mathematics. Many easily stated problems remain open simply because they are isolated, ad hoc curiosities; their difficulty reflects a lack of underlying structure, meaning a proof might settle a lone fact without illuminating anything broader. By contrast, prized conjectures sit at the crossroads of major disciplines and carry sweeping implications. The Riemann Hypothesis, for instance, underpins hundreds of conditional theorems while bridging prime numbers, complex analysis, geometry, and physics. Equally important is a problem’s fertility as an engine for invention. David Hilbert famously compared Fermat’s Last Theorem to a goose that lays golden eggs: the equation itself mattered far less than the rich machinery—from algebraic number theory to modularity—forged in pursuit of it. Ultimately, researchers care most about conjectures that serve as diagnostic benchmarks, where resistance to proof signals a fundamental gap in existing theory and any eventual solution promises to unlock entire new mathematical landscapes.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Simple statement isn't what makes a conjecture matter. What matters is how much it's tied to the rest of mathematics. The Riemann Hypothesis is valued because hundreds of results about prime distribution, error terms and L-functions are proved conditionally on it, and because it sits inside a wider web of ideas, from the Weil conjectures to random matrix theory, that hints at deep hidden structure. Fermat's Last Theorem looked like a curiosity until it was linked to the modularity of elliptic curves. Wiles's proof then changed number theory.

Many conjectures that sound just as simple are isolated. A random claim about the digits of π or about some odd integer sequence may be true by accident, with no reason behind it. Proving it would probably teach us nothing new. Mathematicians value problems that act as "test cases" for whether our theories are adequate. Their solutions tend to require new tools, such as schemes, modular forms or the Langlands program, that then spread across other fields. The Collatz conjecture shows the difference. Erdős warned that "mathematics is not yet ready" for it, so it's famous, but many researchers avoid it because it seems disconnected from the methods that could crack it.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Mathematicians prioritize certain conjectures not because they are harder or simpler to state, but because of their structural centrality and generative power. A conjecture like the Riemann Hypothesis or the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture sits at the crossroads of major theories; hundreds of conditional theorems already depend on it, so a proof would immediately unlock a cascade of results across multiple fields. Just as importantly, researchers care about what a proof would force mathematics to discover. The true value of Fermat's Last Theorem lay less in the equation itself than in the deep bridge between elliptic curves and modular forms built to settle it. Famous conjectures also act as diagnostic stress tests: when our best frameworks fail to resolve them, they expose fundamental gaps in understanding. By contrast, an equally elementary puzzle like the Collatz conjecture often feels isolated from broader theory, offering little conceptual leverage or new machinery even if someone solved it tomorrow.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A conjecture’s simplicity tells you how easy it is to state. Its importance depends on what a solution would explain, what other results depend on it, and what new methods a proof might introduce.

For example, the Riemann hypothesis would sharply constrain how much the distribution of primes can deviate from its expected pattern. Many other results in number theory are already known to follow if it is true. The Collatz conjecture is even easier to state and has attracted substantial attention, but fewer established results depend on it. A proof could still make it more central by revealing a technique that works on other problems.

Attention also has a social history. A conjecture can become a meeting point for a field because generations of researchers have built partial results, found connections, and developed tools around it. Some of that attention reflects consequences mathematicians can already see, and some reflects their judgment about what the search for a proof might uncover.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A conjecture can be easy to state and hard to settle without having much bearing on other questions. Researchers tend to care most when an answer would change what they understand elsewhere. The Riemann hypothesis, for example, predicts how tightly the count of primes up to a given number tracks a known approximation. A proof would settle many results that currently depend on that prediction. A counterexample would reveal a flaw in a remarkably successful picture of how primes are distributed.

A conjecture can also earn attention through what people discover while trying to solve it. Even a failed approach may produce a technique that works on a whole family of other problems. Fame plays a part, too. Once a community shares a question, newcomers can build on earlier attempts, and progress has a ready audience. Simplicity helps explain why a conjecture is memorable. Its connections, consequences, and history help explain why mathematicians devote decades to it.
